W14. Designing Your Own Project

Author

Eunji Ha

Published

August 18, 2026

Note🎯 Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • Narrow a broad interest into a question with a comparison, a measurement and a data source
  • ⚠️ Judge feasibility honestly, and recognise the quadrant where most first projects die
  • Plan four figures before running any analysis
  • State which rung of the evidence ladder your project can reach, and name the next one
  • ⚠️ Say why a negative result is a complete project
  • Leave with a written one-page protocol

🤔 Motivating question

You have one afternoon a week for six months. What is worth doing with it?

1. Narrowing the Question 🎯

A usable question names four things:

  • The population — which patients, at which point in their care
  • The comparison — what against what
  • The measurement — what you will actually quantify
  • The data source — where it comes from, and whether it already exists

⚠️ If any of the four is missing, you have an interest, not a project.

TipThe sentence template

“In ____ [population], is ____ [measurement] different between ____ and ____ [comparison], using ____ [data source]?”

If you cannot fill every blank, the missing blank is your next task — and it is usually not an analysis task. It is a phone call to pathology, or an hour in a public database.

2. ⚠️ Feasibility, Honestly 🗺️

1) What “data you already have” actually includes

Residents consistently underestimate this list:

  • ✅ The pathology archive — FFPE blocks with linked outcomes. Spatial and proteomics both work on FFPE (🔗 W7 §2.2)
  • ✅ Residual clinical samples — banked serum or plasma, under existing consent in some institutions
  • ✅ The EHR — labs, imaging reports, medications, outcomes, already digital
  • ✅ Public data collected for another purpose — GEO, CELLxGENE, TCGA, the UK Biobank return files. A dataset generated to answer question A very often contains the answer to your question B
  • ✅ Your department’s own past studies — data that was analysed once, for one aim

💡 The best resident projects usually combine one existing dataset with one clinical question nobody in the original study cared about.

2) The honest costs

Step Realistic time
IRB / ethics for archived samples ⚠️ 1–4 months, and it starts the clock
Locating and pulling blocks 2–6 weeks, and someone must do it
Sectioning, QC (DV200) 2–4 weeks
Assay turnaround at a core 4–12 weeks
Analysis ⚠️ Always longer than planned
Writing Longer still

⚠️ Start the ethics application in week one. It is the only step that cannot be compressed by working harder.

3. Plan the Figures First 🖼️

1) Name your rung

From 🔗 W8 §3: description → hypothesis → consistent with → supported → demonstrated.

A resident project realistically reaches ③ consistent with. That is publishable, fundable, and honest — provided you say so and name the experiment that would take it to ④ or ⑤.

⚠️ What sinks projects at review is not stopping at ③. It is writing ⑤’s verb over ③’s evidence.

2) ✅ A negative result is a complete project

TipWhat makes a negative result complete

Not “we found nothing”. Rather:

  • ✅ The hypothesis was specific enough to be wrong
  • ✅ The design could have detected the effect — say how large an effect you had power for
  • ✅ The measurement worked — positive controls behaved as expected
  • ✅ You can say what you would do differently

→ That is a better contribution than a fishing expedition that found a p-value. And in a fourteen-week course, it is a much more achievable target.

4. The One-Page Protocol 📄

Write this before you touch data. One page, ten headings.

1. Question        one sentence, with all four blanks filled
2. Why it matters  the decision it would change, in the clinic
3. Population      inclusion, exclusion, and how many exist
4. Comparison      group A vs group B, and how they are matched
5. Measurement     platform, assay, what is quantified
6. n               and what the unit of replication is  ⚠️
7. Confounders     batch, collection site, tube type, operator — and the plan
8. Analysis        the primary test, decided now, not after seeing the data
9. Figures         four captions, written as sentences with blanks
10. What would make me abandon this
ImportantHeading 10 is the one people skip, and the one that saves months

Decide now what result would make you stop.

  • “If fewer than 25 blocks have adequate DV200, the study is not powered and I stop”
  • “If the positive control does not separate, the assay is not working and I stop”
  • “If the effect is smaller than X, it cannot change management and I stop”

⚠️ Written in advance, this is a protocol. Decided afterwards, it is rationalisation.

5. Workshop 💻

1) Ten minutes each, in pairs

  • ① State your question in one sentence. Your partner repeats it back. Did they get it right?
  • ② Which quadrant is it in (§2)? Be honest
  • ③ Sketch Figure 2 — the answer figure — on paper. What are the axes?
  • ④ What is your n, and what is the unit of replication?
  • ⑤ Name one confounder that could produce your expected result on its own
  • ⑥ Heading 10 — what would make you stop?
WarningThe three failure modes you will hear most often today
  • ❌ Too broad. “I want to look at the immune microenvironment.” → apply §1 until a comparison appears
  • ❌ n is wrong. “I have 40,000 cells.” → from how many patients? (🔗 W5 §5)
  • ❌ Data does not exist yet. “I’ll collect fresh samples.” → how many will you have in six months? Usually the honest number is under ten

2) Before the final session

Deliverables:

  • ✅ One-page protocol, all ten headings
  • ✅ Figure 1 (cohort) drafted, even roughly
  • ✅ Figure 2 (the answer) drafted — or the caption with the number still blank
  • ✅ A Quarto document that renders, with no hand-typed numbers (🔗 W2 §3)
  • ✅ Code in a git repository (🔗 W2 §4) — ⚠️ with rawdata/ in .gitignore

Presentation: 15 minutes + 5 minutes questions.

Background            2 min   the clinical problem
Question              1 min   one sentence, and why it is answerable
Data & methods        3 min   what you had, what you did, what you excluded
Results             5–7 min   your four figures, one message each
Interpretation        2 min   which rung, and what would move it up
Clinical implication  1 min   what changes if this is true

6. Where This Leaves You 🎓

You started this course able to run bulk RNA-seq and produce a gene list.

You can now read a GWAS and say what it does not show; judge whether a PRS applies to your patients; tell when a single-cell paper has confused cells with donors; ask where in the tissue something happened; know that the protein may never have been made; recognise a network hub as a publication artifact; and see the wrong control group before anyone runs a statistic.

None of that is coding. All of it is judgment — and it is the part that could not be delegated.

TipThe three habits worth keeping
  • ✅ Ask what the unit of replication is. In every paper, every meeting, every design. It is the single highest-yield question in this field
  • ✅ Look up whether the answer already exists before generating data. One hour in the browser, routinely, has saved entire grants
  • ✅ Write the caption first. For a figure, a paper, or a project — if the sentence is vague, the work will be

💡 And one more: when a result looks too clean, ask what the design would have produced if the hypothesis were false.

📝 Summary

  • A usable question names a population, a comparison, a measurement and a data source
  • ⚠️ Missing one of the four means you have an interest, not a project
  • ✅ Start in the high-value, high-feasibility quadrant: archived samples with outcomes, or public data asked a new question
  • ⚠️ Start the ethics application in week one — it is the step that cannot be compressed
  • ✅ Plan four figures before analysing: cohort · the answer · the mechanism · the implication
  • ✅ Name the rung of the evidence ladder you can reach, and the experiment that moves it up
  • ✅ A negative result is complete if the hypothesis was specific and the design could have detected the effect
  • ⚠️ Write “what would make me abandon this” in advance. Afterwards it is rationalisation
  • ✅ Three habits: ask about the unit of replication, check whether the answer exists, write the caption first

🔑 Key terms

Term One-line meaning
Scoping Narrowing an interest into an answerable question
Unit of replication What you can independently repeat — usually the patient
Feasibility Whether the data can exist within your timeline
One-page protocol The ten headings, written before touching data
Stopping rule The result that would make you abandon the project
Evidence ladder Description → hypothesis → consistent with → supported → demonstrated
Positive control A signal you already know is there, proving the assay worked
Pre-specification Deciding the analysis before seeing the data
